events.title: Safari 4 beta released
events.summary: Apple released Safari 4 beta on February 24, 2009 with Top Sites, Cover Flow tabs, and improved HTML5 and CSS support.
events.about: Safari 4 previewed features that defined Apple's browser for years: a new tab bar, developer tools, and Nitro JavaScript engine improvements. It kept Safari competitive with Chrome and Firefox during the browser performance wars.

narrative.whyChosen: Safari 4 set the template for Apple's browser UX before the mobile-first era.
narrative.whyImportant: Nitro JS and HTML5 push made WebKit a benchmark for speed on Mac.
narrative.problemSolved: Safari 3 felt dated against Chrome's fast release cycle and developer tools.

events.title: Redis first released
events.summary: Salvatore Sanfilippo open-sourced Redis on February 26, 2009 — an in-memory data structure store used as cache, queue, and lightweight database.
events.about: Redis holds strings, lists, sets, and sorted sets in RAM with optional persistence — `GET`/`SET` for sessions, pub/sub for chat, sorted sets for leaderboards. GitHub, Instagram, and Sidekiq queues ran on it. Typical pattern: Postgres for truth, Redis for hot keys and rate limits.

narrative.whyChosen: Redis made in-memory data structures a standard layer in web architecture.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved a single-threaded event loop plus clever structures could scale caching and messaging.
narrative.problemSolved: Relational databases were too slow for session stores, counters, and real-time feeds at web scale.

events.title: MongoDB first released
events.summary: 10gen released MongoDB on February 11, 2009 — a document database storing JSON-like BSON with flexible schemas.
events.about: MongoDB stores documents in collections instead of fixed SQL tables — good for evolving product schemas, content catalogs, and mobile sync. Teams use it with Mongoose in Node or the native driver in Python. Example: user profiles with nested addresses without ALTER TABLE migrations.

narrative.whyChosen: MongoDB led the NoSQL wave for developers who wanted schema flexibility and horizontal scaling.
narrative.whyImportant: It made document stores mainstream alongside relational SQL for web backends.
narrative.problemSolved: Rigid SQL schemas and vertical scaling hurt fast-moving product teams building JSON-heavy apps.
